title: International Date Line: Where the Day Changes
description: Explore the International Date Line — why it zigzags, the 21-hour Diomede gap, and which places greet each new day first. Free interactive map.
summary_sentence: For example, the two Diomede Islands sit under 4 km apart in the Bering Strait — yet their clocks differ by 21 hours, because the date line runs between them.
quick_answer: The International Date Line tool maps the invisible boundary where one calendar day becomes the next. Explore its famous bends around island nations, the 21-hour gap between the Diomede Islands, and why crossing it adds or removes a whole day from your trip.
steps_intro: The line is a political drawing on a geographic idea — here is how it actually runs:

body.t: Fly Sydney to Los Angeles and you land before you left, on paper. Seeing where the line bends around Fiji, Tonga and Samoa explains real itinerary dates. The
shows the solar logic underneath the politics.
Students think the line sits at 180°. Showing Kiribati's great eastern bulge — a whole nation moved the line in 1995 — teaches that time is negotiated, not just measured.
Auckland and Honolulu are close on the map and nearly a day apart on the calendar. The line's position decides whose Monday your email lands in.
First sunrise of the new year, the island that skipped a Friday — the date line generates the best geography questions ever asked.
Big Diomede (Russia) keeps UTC+12; Little Diomede (USA), under 4 km away, keeps UTC−9. The difference is 21 hours — so from the American island you can literally see tomorrow across the water.

On 30 December 2011 Samoa jumped the line westward to align with Australia and New Zealand trade — the country went to sleep on Thursday and woke on Saturday. Friday 30 December simply never happened there.

popular_table.note: There is no international treaty fixing the line — it is drawn by national choices and chart conventions. The maximum clock difference on Earth is 26 hours, between UTC+14 (Kiritimati) and UTC−12 (Baker Island).

faq: Why does no country sit split in two by the line?

Because every country gets to choose its side. The line bends around national territory precisely so that no state wakes up with two dates — the wishes of the countries it passes are the whole reason the zigzags exist.
What happens on a ship crossing the line?
Crews adjust the ship's calendar at a convenient moment near the line — westbound, a day is skipped; eastbound, a day repeats. The adjustment is tradition and logistics, not law.
Is the date line the same as the 180° meridian?
No. The meridian is geometry; the line is a negotiated path that mostly follows it but bends around island groups and national borders — in Kiribati's case by thousands of kilometres.
Can two places share a clock time but different dates?

Yes — that is the line's whole job. Samoa (UTC+13/+14) and American Samoa (UTC−11) are near neighbours with clocks roughly a day apart, which is why the Samoan jump in 2011 split the two Samoas' calendars.
Why did Kiribati move the line?

Before 1995 the line split Kiribati, so its far-flung islands lived on different days — government offices effectively shared only four working days a week. The 1995 bend unified the national calendar.
Does Antarctica have a date line?
Antarctica has no official time zones; research stations keep the time of their supply countries. The date line runs to the South Pole on charts, but no community lives by it there.
